assumptions: The initial product category has enough recurring dossier intake and specialist review cost for workflow software to create material savings.
A responsible-person firm can authorize access to merchant evidence and channel data while retaining specialist judgment and underlying product-safety duties.
Qualified partner staff, rather than the founder, perform document acceptance and every incident decision that requires product-safety expertise.
Required marketplace and commerce-channel fields are sufficiently accessible for a partner-specific implementation, even if some integrations remain partly manual.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A paid, time-bounded deployment with a responsible-person firm in one named category showing committed dossier volume, baseline and post-deployment review labor, implementation and support cost, accepted-dossier contribution, channel error rates, alert-match precision and recall, partner acquisition effort, and renewal intent at an agreed price.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: Moving from commoditized GPSR field storage to the responsible-person firm's dossier-acceptance gate is a coherent insight: provenance, reviewer decisions, and channel-ready records are closer to a costly compliance workflow than raw alerts are. The packet does not establish that this gate is underserved or sufficiently standardized.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Regulatory duties and the risk of listings becoming unavailable create real urgency, but the proposed payer is the responsible-person firm rather than the affected merchant. No evidence shows the firm's dossier or incident workload, current labor cost, purchasing authority, or willingness to buy rather than build or bundle the workflow.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: A workspace plus accepted-dossier usage model can align revenue with recurring operational value, and assigning qualified review to the partner limits direct labor. Pricing, throughput, gross margin, integration cost, support burden, acquisition cost, retention, payback, and realistic owner earnings are all unknown, while inexpensive catalog tools constrain the value attributable to basic data transport.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: One high-risk category and responsible-person firms serving that category form a legible beachhead with a specific workflow owner. The packet does not identify the category, number of suitable firms, annual dossier volume, incident volume, or obtainable revenue, so its economic significance is unresolved.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Embedding at an acceptance gate could create a strong operational position within an individual partner. However, native marketplace workflows, feed vendors, GPSR apps, and the responsible-person firms themselves can extend into this functionality, and there is no exclusive channel, proprietary right, or demonstrated category leadership.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A successful category deployment could extend to additional responsible-person firms, adjacent categories, commerce channels, and other evidence-maintenance obligations. Each expansion may require new specialist rules, integrations, and reviewer processes, so the first implementation may not transfer cheaply.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Embedded workflows and a category-specific history of resolved deficiencies and reviewer decisions could produce switching costs and better templates. The raw alert feed is public, cross-merchant reuse rights are uncertain, identifying data can be incomplete, and incumbents or partners can copy the workflow, leaving the proposed moat conditional and narrow.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Provenance checks, controlled acceptance, and human-reviewed incident routing are more relevant to specialist operations than generic field-entry tools. No measured reduction in review time, listing disruption, error rate, or liability exposure shows that the offer is materially better than a partner's current process plus inexpensive software.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: GPSR obligations are active, marketplace consequences are concrete, and Safety Gate activity sustains compliance attention. The regulation is no longer at its initial transition point, and major platforms and software vendors already support GPSR workflows, reducing the remaining window for a generic entrant.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Selling through a responsible-person firm can aggregate many merchants and reduce direct merchant acquisition, which fits the founder's constraints. No partner commitment, conversion evidence, sales-cycle data, channel economics, or repeatable acquisition route is present, and dependence on a few firms creates substantial bargaining and concentration risk.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The founder's data and automation skills fit provenance, entity resolution, and workflow software, while the partner boundary avoids making the founder the product-safety expert. Execution still depends on obtaining a credible partner, changing integrations, reliable document handling, human review capacity, data permissions, careful liability positioning, and a support load compatible with part-time work.

highest_value_structural_change: Make recurring dossier acceptance and measurable reviewer-labor reduction the paid core, with Safety Gate matching only a human-reviewed add-on, and bind the first deployment to a minimum-volume partner agreement with explicit evidence-access and reusable-pattern rights.
main_structural_strength: The offer occupies the responsible-person firm's dossier-acceptance gate, combining specialist-owned judgment, merchant aggregation, provenance records, and channel release in a workflow that is more valuable and founder-compatible than a horizontal merchant field store.
primary_score_limiter: There is no evidence that responsible-person firms have enough costly, recurring dossier work to support attractive pricing and contribution after integration, rule maintenance, support, and qualified review, or that they will embed an external vendor rather than build or bundle the capability.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Major commerce platforms already provide native or bulk GPSR workflows, while general feed and GPSR products support thousands or unlimited products for roughly EUR 59-89 or USD 79.99 per month; this demonstrates commoditization and price pressure around the record-and-transport layer from which the proposed workflow must clearly separate itself.
